prompt: The bar chart below shows the average number of daily portions of fruit and vegetables consumed by men and women across five age brackets in Country A. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Average Daily Fruit and Vegetable Portions by Age Group and Sex in Country A

keyFeatures.textEn: Daily fruit and vegetable intake rose steadily with age for both sexes until peaking in the 50-64 bracket, before declining slightly among adults aged 65+.
Women consumed more daily portions than men in every single age group by a remarkably consistent margin of 0.7 to 0.9 portions.
Women aged 50-64 recorded the highest consumption overall at 5.1 portions per day, the only group to surpass five portions.
Young men aged 18-24 consumed the fewest portions at 2.4 per day, well below young women in the same bracket (3.2).
In the oldest bracket (65+), intake dipped modestly for both women (4.6) and men (3.9), yet remained higher than in all brackets under 50.

overviewModels: Overall, women consistently ate more fruit and vegetables than men across every age bracket, maintaining a very steady advantage throughout. For both sexes, consumption climbed progressively with age to peak in late middle age before easing slightly among the oldest adults.

In general, daily intake followed an almost parallel trajectory for men and women, rising steadily from young adulthood to the 50-64 cohort and dipping mildly thereafter. Women outperformed men in every bracket, with the youngest adults recording the lowest averages.

Taken as a whole, age and sex both shaped dietary habits in Country A: older adults consumed considerably more portions than younger cohorts, and women outpaced men at every life stage by a consistent margin.
overviewKeyPhrases: easing slightly among the oldest adults

band8Model.text:
The bar chart compares average daily fruit and vegetable consumption among men and women across five adult age brackets in Country A.

Overall, women consistently ate more daily portions than men in every age group, maintaining a steady advantage throughout. For both sexes, intake climbed progressively from young adulthood to a peak in late middle age before easing slightly among the oldest cohort.

The lowest figures occurred in the 18-24 group, where men averaged just 2.4 portions per day compared with 3.2 for women. Consumption then rose steadily across the next two brackets: men increased from 3.1 portions among those aged 25-34 to 3.6 in the 35-49 bracket, while women advanced from 3.9 to 4.5, widening the sex gap slightly from 0.8 to 0.9 portions.

Both sexes reached their maximum intake in the 50-64 cohort, with women averaging 5.1 portions and men 4.2, making older middle-aged women the sole group to exceed five daily portions. Among residents aged 65+, averages dipped modestly to 4.6 portions for women and 3.9 for men, narrowing the gap to 0.7 portions while still exceeding all younger brackets.
